source_text: Ἐκεῖνο ἔτι καὶ νῦν ἐνυπάρχον τῇ γῇ τὸ πρόσ ταγμα, ἐπείγει αὐτὴν καθ' ἑκάστην ἔτους περίοδον ἐξάγειν τὴν δύναμιν ἑαυτῆς ὅσην ἔχει πρός τε βοτανῶν καὶ σπερμάτων καὶ δένδρων γένεσιν. Ὡς γὰρ οἱ στρόβιλοι ἐκ τῆς πρώτης αὐτοῖς ἐνδοθείσης πληγῆς τὰς ἐφεξῆς ποιοῦνται περιστροφὰς, ὅταν πήξαντες τὸ κέντρον ἐν ἑαυτοῖς περιφέρωνται· οὕτω καὶ ἡ τῆς φύσεως ἀκολουθία ἐκ τοῦ πρώτου προστάγματος τὴν ἀρχὴν δεξαμένη, πρὸς πάντα τὸν ἐφεξῆς διεξέρχεται χρόνον, μέχρις ἂν πρὸς τὴν κοινὴν συντέλειαν τοῦ παντὸς καταντήσῃ. Ἐφ' ἣν καὶ ἡμεῖς πάντες ἔγκαρποι καὶ πλήρεις ἔργων ἀγαθῶν ἐπειγώμεθα, ἵνα φυτευθέντες ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ Κυρίου, ἐν ταῖς αὐλαῖς τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἐξανθήσωμεν, ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν, ᾧ ἡ δόξα καὶ τὸ κράτος εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων. Ἀμήν. ΟΜΙΛΙΑ Ϛʹ Περὶ γενέσεως φωστήρων. 6.1 Τὸν ἀθλητῶν θεατὴν μετέχειν τινὸς προσῆκε καὶ αὐτὸν εὐτονίας. Καὶ τοῦτο ἐκ τῶν πανηγυρικῶν θεσμῶν ἄν τις κατίδοι, οἳ τοὺς συγκαθεζομένους εἰς τὸ στάδιον γυμνῇ καθῆσθαι τῇ κεφαλῇ διαγορεύουσιν· ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν, ἵνα μὴ θεατὴς μόνον ἀγωνιστῶν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀγωνιστὴς ἕκαστος αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ μέρει τυγχάνῃ. Οὕτω τοίνυν καὶ τὸν τῶν μεγάλων καὶ ὑπερφυῶν θεαμάτων ἐξεταστὴν, καὶ τὸν τῆς ἄκρας ὄντως καὶ ἀπορρήτου σοφίας ἀκροατὴν προσῆκεν οἴκοθεν ἔχειν ἥκοντά τινας ἀφορμὰς πρὸς τὴν θεωρίαν τῶν προκειμένων, καὶ κοινωνεῖν ἐμοὶ τῆς ἀγωνίας εἰς δύναμιν, οὐχὶ κριτὴν μᾶλλον ἢ συναγωνιστὴν παρεστῶτα· μήποτε ἄρα διαλάθῃ ἡμᾶς τῆς ἀληθείας ἡ εὕρεσις, καὶ τὸ ἐμὸν σφάλμα κοινὴ ζημία τῶν ἀκουόντων γένηται. Πρὸς οὖν τί ταῦτα λέγω; Ὅτι ἐπειδὴ πρόκειται ἡμῖν εἰς τὴν τοῦ κόσμου σύστασιν ἐξέτασις καὶ θεωρία τοῦ παντὸς, οὐκ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου σοφίας τὰς ἀρχὰς ἔχουσα, ἀλλ' ἐξ ὧν τὸν ἑαυτοῦ θεράποντα ὁ Θεὸς ἐξεπαίδευσεν, ἐν εἴδει λαλήσας πρὸς αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐ δι' αἰνιγμάτων, ἀνάγκη που πάντως, τοὺς τῶν μεγάλων φιλοθεάμονας μὴ ἀγύμναστον ἔχειν τὸν νοῦν πρὸς τὴν τῶν προκειμένων ἡμῖν κατανόησιν. Εἴ ποτε οὖν ἐν αἰθρίᾳ νυκτερινῇ πρὸς τὰ ἄρρητα κάλλη τῶν ἄστρων ἐνατενίσας, ἔννοιαν ἔλαβες τοῦ τεχνίτου τῶν ὅλων, τίς ὁ τοῖς ἄνθεσι τούτοις διαποικίλας τὸν οὐρανὸν, καὶ ὅπως ἐν τοῖς ὁρωμένοις πλέον τοῦ τερπνοῦ τὸ ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι· πάλιν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εἰ νήφοντι τῷ λογισμῷ κατέμαθες τὰ τῆς ἡμέρας θαύματα, καὶ διὰ τῶν ὁρωμένων ἀνελογίσω τὸν οὐχ ὁρώμενον, ἐμπαράσκευος ἥκεις ἀκροατὴς καὶ πρέπων τῷ πληρώματι τοῦ σεμνοῦ τούτου καὶ μακαρίου θεάτρου. Δεῦρο δὴ οὖν, ὥσπερ οἱ τοὺς ἀήθεις τῶν πόλεων τῆς χειρὸς λαβόμενοι περιηγοῦνται, οὕτω δὴ καὶ αὐτὸς ἐπὶ τὰ κεκρυμμένα θαύματα ὑμᾶς τῆς μεγάλης ταύτης πόλεως ξεναγήσω. Ἐν τῇ πόλει ταύτῃ, ἐν ᾗ ἡ ἀρχαία πατρὶς ἡμῶν, ἧς μετανέστησεν ἡμᾶς ὁ ἀνθρωποκτόνος δαίμων, τοῖς ἑαυτοῦ δελεάσμασιν ἀνδραποδίσας τὸν ἄνθρωπον· ἐνταῦθα κατόψει τὴν πρώτην τοῦ ἀνθρώπου γένεσιν, καὶ τὸν εὐθὺς ἡμᾶς ἐπικαταλαβόντα θάνατον· ὃν ἐγέννησεν ἡ ἁμαρτία, τὸ πρωτότοκον ἔκγονον τοῦ ἀρχεκάκου δαίμονος. Καὶ γνωρίσεις σαυτὸν, γήϊνον μὲν τῇ φύσει, ἔργον δὲ θείων χειρῶν· δυνάμει μὲν καὶ παραπολὺ τῶν ἀλόγων λειπόμενον, ἄρχοντα δὲ χειροτονητὸν τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ τῶν ἀψύχων.
thought_title: The command still drives the earth, and the hearer must come prepared
orientation: Basil is closing his homily on the third day's vegetation and opening the sixth homily, on the creation of the lights, by urging his hearers to come as fellow contestants, not mere judges.
pass_a_gloss: That command, still even now existing in the earth, urges it according to each year's cycle to bring out its own power, as much as it has, for the generation of plants and seeds and trees. For just as tops, from the first blow given to them, make their subsequent rotations, whenever, having fixed the point in themselves, they spin around; so also the sequence of nature, having received its beginning from the first command, passes through all subsequent time, until it arrives at the common completion of the whole. Toward which may we all also, fruitful and full of good works, hasten, so that, having been planted in the house of the Lord, in the courts of our God we may bloom, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be the glory and the might unto the ages of the ages. Amen. Homily 6. On the generation of the lights. 6.1 It was fitting that the spectator of athletes should himself also share in some vigor. And this one might observe from the festival laws, which prescribe that those sitting together in the stadium sit with bare head; in my opinion, so that each may be not only a spectator of contestants, but also himself a contestant in his turn. So then also the examiner of great and extraordinary spectacles, and the hearer of truly highest and ineffable wisdom, it was fitting to have come from home with some starting points for the contemplation of the things set before us, and to share with me in the struggle as far as possible, standing by not as a judge rather than as a fellow contestant; lest perhaps the discovery of the truth escape us, and my error become a common loss of the hearers. Why then do I say these things? Because since the examination of the constitution of the world and the contemplation of the whole is set before us, having its beginnings not from the wisdom of the world, but from what God taught his own servant, speaking to him in visible form, and not through riddles, it is altogether necessary, I suppose, that those who love to behold great things not have an untrained mind for the comprehension of the things set before us. If ever then in clear night air, having gazed at the ineffable beauties of the stars, you received a thought of the craftsman of all things, who is the one who adorned the heaven with these flowers, and how in the things seen the necessary is more than the delightful; again by day, if with sober reasoning you learned the wonders of the day, and through the things seen you reasoned by analogy to the one not seen, you have come as a prepared hearer and one fitting for the fullness of this august and blessed theater. Come then, just as those who take by the hand those unfamiliar with cities lead them around, so also I myself will guide you as a stranger to the hidden wonders of this great city. In this city, in which is our ancient fatherland, from which the man-slaying demon removed us, having enslaved man by his own baits; here you will see the first origin of man, and the death that immediately overtook us; which sin begot, the firstborn offspring of the evil-originating demon. And you will know yourself, earthly in nature, but a work of divine hands; in power indeed falling far short of the irrational creatures, but appointed ruler of the irrational and the soulless.

choices.english: the command still even now existing in the earth
choices.why: Keeps the present participle force of the command's ongoing immanence in the earth, matching Basil's point that the original creative word remains active.
rejected: the command that is still in the earth
the command still present in the earth

choices.why: Refers to spinning tops, the common ancient toy; 'tops' is the plain English equivalent and preserves the kinetic image Basil uses for nature's ongoing motion.
Renders the causal chain of natural processes set in motion by the first command; 'sequence' captures the ordered succession Basil describes.

choices.english: speaking to him in visible form
choices.why: Basil contrasts God's direct, visible speech to Moses with riddles; 'in visible form' preserves the contrast with indirect or enigmatic communication.
The verb means to reduce to slavery; 'enslaved' keeps the force of the demon's act against humanity.
The term means chosen or appointed by vote or decree; 'appointed' conveys the conferred authority over irrational creatures without implying election by peers.

pass_b_english: That command still even now existing in the earth urges it on, in each yearly cycle, to bring out all the power it has for the generation of plants, seeds, and trees. For just as tops, once the first blow is given them, make their subsequent rotations when they fix their point in themselves and spin around, so too the sequence of nature, having received its beginning from the first command, passes through all the time that follows, until it arrives at the common completion of the universe. Toward that completion may we all press on, fruitful and full of good works, so that, planted in the house of the Lord, we may bloom in the courts of our God, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power forever and ever. Amen.
Homily 6: On the creation of the lights.

A spectator of athletes ought to share in some measure of their vigor. One can see this from the rules of the festivals, which prescribe that those sitting together in the stadium sit with bare heads—in my opinion, so that each person may be not only a spectator of the contestants but also in his own turn a contestant. So too, then, the examiner of great and extraordinary spectacles, and the hearer of truly supreme and ineffable wisdom, ought to come with some resources of his own for the contemplation of what lies before us, and to share in my struggle as far as he is able—standing by not so much as a judge as a fellow contestant. Otherwise the discovery of the truth may escape us, and my error may become a common loss for the hearers.

Why do I say this? Because since our task is the examination of the world's constitution and the contemplation of the universe—a task whose principles come not from the wisdom of the world, but from what God taught his servant, speaking to him plainly and not through riddles—it is altogether necessary that those who love to behold great things not have an untrained mind for the understanding of what lies before us. If ever, then, on a clear night you have gazed at the ineffable beauties of the stars and received a thought of the craftsman of all things—who it is who has adorned the heaven with these flowers, and how in visible things the necessary exceeds the delightful—and again by day, if with sober reasoning you have studied the wonders of the day and through visible things have inferred the invisible one, you have come as a prepared hearer, fit for the fullness of this solemn and blessed theater.

Come then—just as those who take strangers by the hand and lead them around a city—so I myself will guide you through the hidden wonders of this great city. In this city is our ancient homeland, from which the man-slaying demon removed us, having enslaved man by his own enticements. Here you will see the first origin of man, and the death that immediately overtook us—death, which sin bore, the firstborn offspring of the evil-originating demon. And you will come to know yourself: earthly in nature, yet the work of divine hands; in power far inferior to the irrational animals, yet appointed ruler by election of the irrational and the lifeless.

problems.quote: speaking to him in visible form and not through riddles
problems.source_quote: ἐν εἴδει λαλήσας πρὸς αὐτὸν, καὶ οὐ δι' αἰνιγμάτων
problems.why: ἐν εἴδει means 'in plain form/appearance' or 'openly', not 'visible form'; God spoke plainly to Moses, not that God took visible form
problems.fix: speaking to him plainly and not through riddles

edits.old: speaking to him in visible form and not through riddles
edits.new: speaking to him plainly and not through riddles

fixed: Changed 'in visible form' to 'plainly' for ἐν εἴδει, which here means openly/plainly, not visibly.

problems.quote: appointed ruler of the irrational and the lifeless
problems.source_quote: ἄρχοντα δὲ χειροτονητὸν τῶν ἀλόγων καὶ τῶν ἀψύχων
problems.why: Missing 'χειροτονητὸν' (appointed by election/raising of hands), a key term for Basil's theology of human dignity.
problems.fix: appointed ruler by election of the irrational and the lifeless
problems.ruling: χειροτονητὸν means 'appointed by raising hands/election'; 'appointed' drops the specific mode of appointment, a key theological term.

edits.old: appointed ruler of the irrational and the lifeless
edits.new: appointed ruler by election of the irrational and the lifeless

fixed: Added 'by election' to render χειροτονητὸν, which the English omitted.

last_rejected.quote: to bring out all the power it has
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐξάγειν τὴν δύναμιν ἑαυτῆς ὅσην ἔχει
last_rejected.why: Source says 'as much power as it has'; 'all' slightly overstates, but key issue is missing 'ὅσην ἔχει' nuance.
last_rejected.fix: to bring out whatever power it has
last_rejected.ruling: 'all...it has' captures ὅσην ἔχει adequately; 'all' is within normal range for ὅσην.

last_rejected.source_quote: ἐν τοῖς ὁρωμένοις πλέον τοῦ τερπνοῦ τὸ ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστι
last_rejected.why: Reverses the intended meaning: source says necessity surpasses pleasure, not exceeds delight.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Exceeds' can mean 'surpasses'; πλέον τοῦ τερπνοῦ = 'more than the pleasant,' so meaning is preserved.

last_rejected.why: χειροτονητὸν means 'appointed by God's hand/choice,' not human election; obscures divine appointment.
last_rejected.ruling: χειροτονητὸν means 'appointed' (by hand/choice); 'by election' is a valid rendering, not necessarily human.

last_rejected.why: ἀρχέκακος means 'originator/prince of evil,' not 'evil-originating'; misattributes the demon's role.
last_rejected.fix: the demon who is originator of evil
last_rejected.ruling: ἀρχέκακος = 'originator of evil'; 'evil-originating' conveys this adequately, not a major error.
